Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ISO-delivered signed RegSchdTask.exe executed from non-standard/removable path · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — TELESHIM Abuses Telegram for C2 in Attacks Against Middle East Governments
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TELESHIM DLL side-load: RegSchdTask.exe loads rogue AsTaskSched.dll · [LLM] MIXEDKEY encrypted payload: .PCPKEY file dropped on disk · [LLM] TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY/BINDCLOAK known-bad file hash execution · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Telegram Bot API used for C2 by non-browser/non-messaging process · [LLM] BINDCLOAK C2 beacon to cert.hypersnet.com / ssl.blsouqs.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY sideload host binary beacons to Telegram (C2 + exfil)
ISO-delivered signed RegSchdTask.exe executed from non-standard/removable path AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the campaign's initial access: the legitimate ASUS-signed RegSchdTask.exe run from an ISO mount, user Temp, Downloads or Public dir rather than its real ASUS install directory. Article-specific because this binary is the sideload host used to load the TELESHIM DLL. Rationale: Anchored on the named ASUS sideload host RegSchdTask.exe (arrives via ISO) with a path exclusion — a signed scheduler utility running from Temp/ISO is the article's exact initial-access shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-hide-c2-traffic-inside-telegram/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ASUS software portable/troubleshooting run from a technician USB
  • Software packaging/repackaging labs staging ASUS utilities in Temp
  • IT deploying ASUS drivers from a network share extracted to a user path
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","asussetup.exe","asusdownloadlicense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 against the article's hash list and check the parent — a mounted ISO (explorer.exe / DVD drive letter) or archive tool as parent is high-signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the RegSchdTask.exe/AsTaskSched.dll pair from the same folder. 3) Hunt: on the same device pivot to DeviceImageLoadEvents for AsTaskSched.dll and DeviceNetworkEvents to api.telegram.org within the next hour.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "RegSchdTask.exe"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\", @"\Windows\"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\RegSchdTask.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\Program Files" and NewProcessName !has @"\Windows\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TELESHIM DLL side-load: RegSchdTask.exe loads rogue AsTaskSched.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the TELESHIM sideload event itself — the ASUS RegSchdTask.exe process loading a non-Microsoft AsTaskSched.dll from a non-standard path. This is the moment the 32-bit TELESHIM backdoor gets execution inside a trusted process. Rationale: Uses the exact parent/module pair named by Zscaler (RegSchdTask.exe -> AsTaskSched.dll); an ASUS scheduler loading a DLL of that name is unique to this intrusion. Falcon FDR does not ship a module-load event type, hence empty falcon query. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-telegram-bots-secret-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1497
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine ASUS utility shipping a same-named helper DLL after a legitimate update
  • QA/reverse-engineering lab replaying the sample
  • Backup/restore repopulating an old ASUS install folder
  • EDR sensor re-baselining image loads after agent upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not(SHA256 in~ ("")) or FolderPath !has @"\ASUS\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash AsTaskSched.dll and confirm it is unsigned / not signed by ASUSTeK vs the article hashes. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL, and kill the RegSchdTask.exe process tree. 3) Hunt: check the same host/hour for outbound HTTPS to api.telegram.org and for a second sideload pair GoProAlertService.exe + pthreadVC2.dll.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RegSchdTask.exe"
| where FileName =~ "AsTaskSched.dll"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Program Files\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where EventData has "AsTaskSched.dll" and EventData has "RegSchdTask.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData

Telegram Bot API used for C2 by non-browser/non-messaging process AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the core TELESHIM C2 channel: a process that is not a browser or the Telegram desktop client initiating connections to api.telegram.org / core.telegram.org. Article-specific because TELESHIM stores an encrypted bot token + chat ID and beacons to the Telegram Bot API to blend with legitimate traffic. Rationale: Pivots on api.telegram.org/core.telegram.org (confirmed by Zscaler as the TELESHIM C2 host) plus a browser/Telegram-client exclusion so only unexpected processes surface. Sentinel path uses DNS (ImDnsActivity) because process-attributed egress is not natively available in that schema. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-hide-c2-traffic-inside-telegram/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom PowerShell/Python scripts using Telegram bots for internal alerting
  • Monitoring/CI agents posting build status to a Telegram channel
  • curl/wget one-off tests against the Telegram API by a developer
  • Third-party notification middleware bundled in an EXE contacting Telegram
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("python.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell.exe","node.exe","curl.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its signer/hash; a signed ASUS/GoPro utility or an unsigned binary from Temp beaconing to Telegram is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block api.telegram.org egress for that asset group, and capture the process memory for the encrypted bot token/chat ID. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts talking to the Telegram API from the same process name and pivot to BINDCLOAK domains cert.hypersnet.com / ssl.blsouqs.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org","core.telegram.org")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("telegram.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","teams.exe","ms-teams.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.telegram.org","core.telegram.org")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Queries=make_set(DnsQuery) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY sideload host binary beacons to Telegram (C2 + exfil) AIActions on Objectives High
High-fidelity variant scoped to the two named sideload hosts (RegSchdTask.exe, GoProAlertService.exe) sending traffic to the Telegram Bot API. TELESHIM registers the host by MAC and chunk-exfiltrates command output over this channel, so these binaries reaching Telegram is the campaign's C2/exfil signature. Rationale: Two named-binary anchors (RegSchdTask.exe / GoProAlertService.exe) plus the telegram.org destination make this near-zero-FP — neither an ASUS scheduler nor a GoPro alert service has any legitimate reason to reach the Telegram API. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://cyberpress.org/teleshim-targets-middle-east-governments/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated legitimate GoPro desktop service phoning home (not to Telegram — excluded by destination)
  • Endpoint proxy rewriting SNI causing mislabeled RemoteUrl
  • Threat-intel detonation of the sample in a monitored VM
  • Renamed internal utility coincidentally named RegSchdTask.exe on a build box
Response runbook
1) Triage: this pairing is malicious by design — validate the host is impacted, not a sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate immediately, block telegram.org egress for the asset, and preserve process memory to recover the bot token/chat ID for C2 takedown. 3) Hunt: search proxy/DNS org-wide for the same process->telegram.org pattern and correlate with reconnaissance commands (whoami, ipconfig, net) executed 4:00-12:00 UTC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("RegSchdTask.exe","GoProAlertService.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org","core.telegram.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("RegSchdTask.exe","GoProAlertService.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "telegram.org"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MIXEDKEY encrypted payload: .PCPKEY file dropped on disk AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the environmentally-keyed final payload MIXEDKEY reflectively loads — files with the unusual .PCPKEY extension (e.g. C99F29AC08454855B3D538960BB2F34F.PCPKEY). The extension is unique to this campaign and encrypted with a key derived from the volume serial number. Rationale: The .PCPKEY extension (with the concrete sample C99F29AC08454855B3D538960BB2F34F.PCPKEY) is a bespoke campaign artifact with no legitimate software use, making a bare extension match high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-telegram-bots-secret-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1620 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated proprietary app coincidentally using a .PCPKEY extension (rare)
  • Backup software copying a previously dropped payload during restore
  • Forensic tooling writing a captured sample back to disk during analysis
  • EDR quarantine restore recreating the file
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess writing the .PCPKEY file — GoProAlertService.exe or pthreadVC2.dll context confirms MIXEDKEY. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the .PCPKEY file plus the GoProAlertService.exe/pthreadVC2.dll pair. 3) Hunt: pivot to the parent sideload (RegSchdTask.exe/TELESHIM) and outbound BINDCLOAK C2 to cert.hypersnet.com; collect the volume serial number for payload decryption.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".PCPKEY"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".PCPKEY"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BINDCLOAK C2 beacon to cert.hypersnet.com / ssl.blsouqs.com AICommand & Control High
Detects the final-stage BINDCLOAK implant contacting its C2 infrastructure. Article-specific IOC-driven detection on the confirmed BINDCLOAK domain cert.hypersnet.com plus the campaign domain ssl.blsouqs.com, covering both resolution (DNS) and connection telemetry. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the two second-source-confirmed campaign domains (cert.hypersnet.com is BINDCLOAK's named C2). Sentinel path corrected to DnsEvents.Name (IPAddresses is not a DnsEvents column). Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1 • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-hide-c2-traffic-inside-telegram/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Passive DNS/threat-intel scanner resolving the IOC domain from a research host
  • Security appliance sinkhole logging the domain
  • Analyst manually browsing the IOC for validation
  • DNS logging duplicate from a forwarder replaying old queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and host; any internal asset resolving cert.hypersnet.com/ssl.blsouqs.com outside a sanctioned research VM is a confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block both domains at DNS and proxy, and snapshot memory for the 64-bit BINDCLOAK implant. 3) Hunt: trace back the TELESHIM->MIXEDKEY->BINDCLOAK chain on the host and sweep for other assets resolving the same domains or matching the sample hashes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("cert.hypersnet.com","ssl.blsouqs.com")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("cert.hypersnet.com","ssl.blsouqs.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY/BINDCLOAK known-bad file hash execution AIInstallation Medium
IOC hash sweep for the campaign's PE samples across process creation, module loads and file writes. Surfaces any host that executed or wrote a TELESHIM, MIXEDKEY or BINDCLOAK sample by SHA256/MD5. Rationale: Hash-based sweep using the 8 SHA256 + 5 MD5 samples from the article's IOC bundle; exact-hash matches are definitionally low-FP and cover process, module-load and file-write surfaces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/targeted-attack-government-entities-middle-east-part-1
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in a monitored lab
  • EDR retro-scan re-hashing a quarantined file
  • Threat-intel platform ingesting the sample into a detonation sandbox on the corporate network
  • Backup indexing a previously captured artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match is a live host not a sandbox, and note which stage (TELESHIM/MIXEDKEY/BINDCLOAK) the hash maps to. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine all matching files, and block the associated Telegram and hypersnet/blsouqs C2. 3) Hunt: expand to the full kill chain on the host (sideload pairs, .PCPKEY drop, C2 beacons) and sweep the fleet for the same hashes and reconnaissance activity in the 4:00-12:00 UTC operator window.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("cert.hypersnet.com", "ssl.blsouqs.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["cert.hypersnet.com", "ssl.blsouqs.com"]);

| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

GitHub Adds 3-Day Dependabot Cooldown to Limit Poisoned Package Adoption

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 5 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has announced a new cooldown mechanism in Dependabot, allowing the tool to wait at least three days after a release is published before opening a pull request. "The cooldown configuration option in the dependabot.yml still controls the behavior, though, so you can choose a different cooldown parameter that fits your project," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

CISA KEV: CVE-2025-68686 — Fortinet FortiOS Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-07-27 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet FortiOS contains an exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor vulnerability. This may allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to bypass the patch developed for the symbolic link persistency mechanism observed in some post-exploit cases, via crafted HTTP requests. An attacker would need first to have compromised the product via another vulnerability, at filesystem level. Vendor: Fortinet, Product: FortiOS. Federal patch due: 2026-08-10.

2026-07-25 16 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malvertising operation dubbed SourTrade is making victims' browsers build the final Windows executable themselves, using a legitimate Bun runtime as its base instead of serving one complete malicious file from a fixed URL. SourTrade malvertising infrastructure contact (campaign domains + Bun-runtime host) AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution / network connections to the published SourTrade landing-page and secondary-runtime domains, including purelogicbox.org which serves the clean Bun runtime. This is the delivery-infrastructure IOC pivot for the browser-assembled malware campaign detailed by Confiant. Rationale: Uses the concrete SourTrade domain IOCs published by Confiant and re-counted by The Hacker News (purelogicbox.org is specifically the Bun-runtime host). Domain-list resolution from a browser is high-fidelity because these are single-purpose malvertising domains with no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-sites-use-javascript-to-build-malware-in-browser-memory/
ATT&CKT1189 T1583.008
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating a SourTrade sample intentionally
  • Threat-intel platform or URL-scanning appliance crawling the IOC domains
  • A future benign re-registration of an expired campaign domain (domains rotate)
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging the block as a query event
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MonitoringHost.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-detonation-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and the initiating browser process; check whether a same-session .exe download landed in Downloads (pivot to UC2). 2) Contain: block the domain(s) at the DNS/proxy layer, isolate the host if an executable was written, and reset any trading/wallet credentials the user may have entered on the fake landing page. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the full 96-domain SourTrade set, look for browser-written .exe files with FileOriginUrl on any campaign domain, and review ad-referral chains that led the user to the landing page.

Browser-assembled SourTrade executable dropped with campaign-domain origin (MotW) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a browser process writing a .exe to disk whose Mark-of-the-Web download source (FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl) is a SourTrade landing-page domain, plus the three published sample hashes. This is the article-specific moment the in-browser-assembled Bun executable lands on disk — the point where per-session hash rotation is defeated by pivoting on origin rather than hash. Rationale: The Defender query pivots on FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl — the MotW record Confiant notes points at the landing page domain, not the Bun-runtime host — which survives the per-session hash rotation the campaign relies on. The three published SHA-256 samples are added as a direct fallback; Splunk/Falcon fall back to browser-written .exe in Downloads because CIM/FDR lack an origin-URL field. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://gbhackers.com/sourtrade-browser-assembled/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html
ATT&CKT1027 T1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers downloaded via browser to Downloads (very common on the hash-less fallback branch)
  • Portable apps or dev tools (e.g. genuine Bun/Node installers) saved by developers
  • Browser auto-update stub executables written to profile folders
  • Corporate software-portal downloads delivering signed .exe installers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe") and isempty(FileOriginUrl) and isempty(FileOriginReferrerUrl) and SHA256 !in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b","05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6","ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileOriginUrl/ReferrerUrl resolves to a SourTrade domain (high-confidence branch) or that the .exe is unsigned/low-prevalence on the Downloads fallback branch; check the process tree for subsequent execution. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the origin domain, and isolate the host if the executable ran; because JSCEAL/WeevilProxy is the likely payload, treat as credential-theft — force-reset the user's trading, wallet, and SSO credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot the origin domain into UC1/UC3, look for a same-origin ServiceWorker /config fetch preceding the write, and scan for Bun-runtime standalone executables launched from Downloads across the fleet.

SourTrade ServiceWorker build-instruction fetch (/config + /sw.js on campaign domains) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts web-proxy requests to the /sw.js ServiceWorker and /config build-instruction endpoints on SourTrade campaign domains — the exact same-origin paths the landing page uses to register the worker and pull the PE header, section table, .bun bytecode and secondary runtime URL. Scoped to the campaign domains, this catches the technique even as individual sample hashes rotate and helps surface newly-registered domains reusing the pattern. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim /sw.js and /config paths (article code blocks) scoped to the confirmed campaign domains — the ServiceWorker + build-instruction pattern is the campaign's signature and survives hash rotation. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because FDR and the available Datadog sources do not carry URL request paths and there is no AWS telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.confiant.com/p/sourtrade-browser-assembled-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sourtrade-malvertising-malware/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/malvertising-sends-malware-in-pieces.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A future benign re-registration of an expired SourTrade domain serving a legitimate /config or /sw.js
  • Proxy logging a blocked request as an allowed event after policy change
  • Security scanner / crawler fetching the campaign paths during investigation
  • Rare legitimate PWA on a re-purposed domain registering a service worker at /sw.js
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host+user made the /config fetch and whether a /sw.js registration and secondary purelogicbox.org runtime fetch occurred in the same session; check for a subsequent browser-written .exe (UC2). 2) Contain: block the domain at the proxy, clear the browser's registered ServiceWorkers on the affected host, and isolate if an executable landed. 3) Hunt: expand to the full 96-domain list, generalize the hunt to any domain where a single client fetched /sw.js then /config then received a same-origin attachment download, and correlate the originating malicious ad-referral.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","campainter.digital","riovera.info","lunavo.club","hanzoa.digital","authcom.digital","fererro.digital","zythera.info","angelxc.digital","toushere.digital","auronix.digital","quorivamesh.digital","junora.digital","savanhe.digital","tenderi.digital")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/config","/sw.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpHostName has_any ("purelogicbox.org","noxani.info","greensite.digital","yuntaro.digital","nexlisa.info","vashiro.info","campainter.digital","riovera.info","lunavo.club","hanzoa.digital","authcom.digital","fererro.digital","zythera.info","angelxc.digital","toushere.digital","auronix.digital","quorivamesh.digital","junora.digital","savanhe.digital","tenderi.digital")
| where Url has_any ("/config","/sw.js")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, FileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

DeviceFileEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:

detection:

        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

references:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows

    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f

        where Web.dest IN ("purelogicbox.org", "noxani.info", "greensite.digital", "yuntaro.digital", "nexlisa.info", "vashiro.info", "campainter.digital", "riovera.info", "lunavo.club", "hanzoa.digital")

        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or SHA1 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976") or MD5 in~ ("9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9a29d26b94b708830c6eaea8a6c17616ec677adaf09114190d0e129564b2ca1b", "05c0d056a6b3e76736d4f378541d28f24ecdf40060eeed24d8aa283d2f0120f6", "ad542ed44df306bdcbb022ae210da74abad74e978cc1e3992016976282f31976"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised PyPI Package: mrmustard 0.7.4 Steals SSH, Cloud, and Kubernetes Credentials

StepSecurity
2026-07-25 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

mrmustard 0.7.4 on PyPI was a credential stealer that ran on import, exfiltrating SSH keys, AWS, and Kubernetes credentials. Here is the analysis, IOCs, and how to respond.

ATT&CKT1027 T1190 T1195.002 T1555.003
Domainsmetrics.femboy.energy femboy.energy

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious mrmustard 0.7.4 artifact by hash or filename
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised PyPI Package: mrmustard 0.7.4 Steals SSH, Cloud, and Kubernetes Cred
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] mrmustard persistence artifacts: mmcompat.pth and .tf_cache/hw_probe.pyc · [LLM] Recurring cron/shell-rc execution of .tf_cache/hw_probe.pyc payload · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] mrmustard stealer C2 exfil to metrics.femboy.energy · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python interpreter reading SSH + AWS + Kube credential stores · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
mrmustard stealer C2 exfil to metrics.femboy.energy AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to the attacker-controlled domain femboy.energy (XOR-decoded C2 https://metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect) used by the trojanised mrmustard 0.7.4 PyPI package to exfiltrate SSH keys, AWS and Kubernetes credentials. The domain is a hard IOC confirmed by two independent vendor writeups, so any resolution or connection to it is high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the hard C2 IOC metrics.femboy.energy / femboy.energy, confirmed by StepSecurity and safedep.io (XOR key tf_compat_v2 decodes to https://metrics.femboy.energy/v1/collect). Datadog left empty: the target hosts are Linux dev/HPC boxes and none of the listed Datadog sources carry Linux DNS/proxy telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-pypi-mrmustard-0-7-4-credential-stealer • https://safedep.io/mrmustard-malicious-pypi-package/
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment scanners or sandboxes deliberately resolving the IOC domain
  • Security researcher reproducing the malware in a lab that reports into production telemetry
  • DNS sinkhole / RPZ appliance logging the blocked query (which is actually a true positive being handled)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (expect a python interpreter or the .cache/.tf_cache/hw_probe.pyc payload); confirm mrmustard 0.7.4 was installed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block femboy.energy at DNS/proxy/firewall, and treat the machine as compromised. 3) Hunt: rotate every SSH key, AWS credential and kube config reachable from the host, then sweep the fleet for mrmustard 0.7.4, the mmcompat.pth file, the */15 cron and the shell-rc marker.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "femboy.energy" or RemoteUrl endswith "femboy.energy"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "femboy.energy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
